# How priority is actually computed here {#sec-priority}

::: {.tldr}
Your position in line is a weighted sum of factors. On MedicineBow the weights are **QOS ×
200, fair-share × 100, job-size × 100, age × 10.** QOS dominates — it's weighted twice
fair-share and twenty times age. Translation: **which QOS you pick matters more than anything
else you do.** You cannot out-wait a better QOS by sitting in the queue.
:::

## The real formula (straight from the machine)

Slurm computes a priority score for every pending job and runs the highest scores first
(subject to backfill, below). The score is a weighted sum, and MedicineBow's actual weights
are:

```text
PriorityWeightQOS       = 200     <- dominant
PriorityWeightFairShare = 100
PriorityWeightJobSize   = 100
PriorityWeightAge       = 10
PriorityWeightPartition = 0       (partition doesn't affect priority here)
```

Each factor is a number between 0 and 1, multiplied by its weight, and summed. So the biggest
lever, by a wide margin, is **QOS**.

## What each factor means for you

**QOS (weight 200) — the big one.** Higher-priority QOS = dramatically better position. From
@sec-partitions: `interactive` (90) > `fast` (80) > `normal` (70) > `long` (60). Choosing
`fast` over `long` is worth more priority than any amount of waiting will earn you. This is
*why* the short-vs-long decision in @sec-queue-times matters so much.

**Fair-share (weight 100) — recent usage.** Slurm tracks how much your account has used
lately, relative to its share. Burn a lot this week and your fair-share factor drops, lowering
priority for a while; it recovers as usage decays (half-life ~7 days here). You can't game
this — it's the mechanism that stops any one group from monopolizing the machine. It rewards
*steady* use over *bursty* hogging.

**Job size (weight 100).** A factor based on the resources requested. Combined with the
`SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME` flag this cluster sets, it interacts with your time request — another
reason not to over-ask (@sec-resources).

**Age (weight 10) — time spent waiting.** Your job slowly gains priority the longer it sits,
maxing out after ~3 days. But at weight 10, age is a tie-breaker, **not** a strategy. You will
not age your way past someone who chose a better QOS. Waiting is the weakest lever there is.

## The one practical takeaway

::: {.callout-important}
## Pick the QOS, don't play the queue
Because QOS is weighted 2× fair-share and 20× age, the highest-leverage thing you can do for
start time is **choose the most appropriate high-priority QOS your job fits into** — the
shortest walltime tier that still lets your job finish (@sec-queue-times). Everything else —
waiting longer, resubmitting, submitting at 3am — is noise by comparison.
:::

## Backfill: why a small job can jump the line

Priority decides the *order*, but Slurm also **backfills**: if the top job is waiting for,
say, 40 nodes to free up, Slurm will slot in a smaller, shorter job that fits in the gap
*right now* — as long as doing so won't delay that top job's reserved start time. This is why
a tiny 20-minute test can start immediately even when the queue looks deep, and it's a big
part of why short jobs feel so much snappier than long ones. Requesting **less time and fewer
resources makes your job backfill-eligible in more gaps** — yet another payoff for
right-sizing.

## Seeing your own priority

```bash
sprio -j <jobid>            # the priority breakdown for a pending job
sprio -l                    # all pending jobs, with factor columns
showjobreasons <jobid>      # ARCC helper: plain-language "why am I waiting?"
```

If `sprio` shows your QOS factor is low because you're on `long`, and the job would actually
finish in 10 hours, resubmitting under `fast` is the single most effective change you can make.

With priority understood, let's watch jobs actually run — and diagnose them when they don't
(@sec-monitoring).
